episode_title: How Can We Make Work Work? | BCG’s Deborah Lovich

real_qa.q: What are the five daily practices in Deborah Lovich's Make Work Work book for employee-centric leaders?
real_qa.r: The five practices are: celebrate someone by giving positive feedback in the moment or end of day; leadership through going to where work happens and finding ways to help; be interested by asking people about themselves as humans and remembering details about their lives; co-create by involving impacted employees in changes from the beginning; and do it first by visibly modeling behaviors you ask your team to adopt before requesting it from them.
real_qa.requete: five daily practices Make Work Work Deborah Lovich

real_qa.q: Why does Deborah Lovich argue employee-centric organizations are seven times more likely to be AI mature?
real_qa.r: Lovich published research in Harvard Business Review with Stephen Meyer from Columbia Business School showing that when organizations approach AI with employee-centric thinking rather than fear-based messaging about job loss or demands for more work with fewer resources, employees actually engage with and adopt AI tools. If you introduce AI as purely a productivity play to reduce headcount, it fails because employees will not engage with tools they believe threaten their employment.
real_qa.requete: employee centric AI maturity Deborah Lovich BCG research

real_qa.q: What percentage of companies is Deborah Lovich estimating are stuck in a transaction trap between employers and employees?
real_qa.r: Based on Lovich's three decades of client experience, she estimates that over 90 percent of companies are stuck in what she calls a transaction trap—an us versus them dynamic that destroys value. Only about 5 to 10 percent of companies truly get employee centricity and actually act on it, with examples including Costco, Trader Joe's, and Delta Airlines.
real_qa.requete: percentage companies transaction trap employee centricity

real_qa.q: How did Delta Airlines demonstrate employee centricity during airline deregulation when prices were dropping?
real_qa.r: When Delta Airlines entered deregulation and faced price pressures, the executives did not fire employees. Instead, executives took salary cuts so they would not be paid more than the highest-paid employee, the pilots. In response, Delta Airlines employees collectively pooled their own money to purchase an aircraft for the company called the Spirit of Delta, demonstrating unprecedented employee commitment.
real_qa.requete: Delta Airlines Spirit of Delta employee ownership deregulation

real_qa.q: Why did leadership lose the flexible work strategy after COVID-19 if it was working for employee engagement?
real_qa.r: Leadership never invested in building the capability and muscle of managers to effectively lead distributed teams, so they reverted to co-location as the default method for building culture, connection, development, coaching, and mentorship. However, Lovich argues those practices were not actually better in physical locations either, since teams were already distributed before COVID through conference calls and remote work patterns.
real_qa.requete: hybrid work distributed teams leadership lost capability COVID

guest.bio_context: Deborah Lovich has spent over 32 years at Boston Consulting Group working on fixing leadership, culture, and flexible workspaces for both office workers and deskless workers. Over the last three years, she conducted extensive research uncovering that employers treat employees as a cost rather than as equally valuable stakeholders like customers and shareholders. She is retiring from BCG but will continue as senior partner emeritus while focusing on promoting employee-centric organizations through her new book, Make Work Work.

real_quote: Employee centric organizations are seven times as likely to be AI mature. Maybe you don't care about employee centricity, but if you care about AI deployment, you better pretend like you care about employee centricity and start acting on it.
key_stats: 32 years: Deborah Lovich's tenure at Boston Consulting Group before retirement
90 plus percent: Companies stuck in a transaction trap dynamic between employers and employees
5 to 10 percent: Percentage of companies that truly get employee centricity and act on it
Seven times: AI-mature likelihood ratio of employee-centric organizations versus non-employee-centric organizations, per BCG and Columbia Business School research published in Harvard Business Review
20 to 40 percent: Proportion of U.S. jobs that can be performed in distributed work settings
60 percent: Proportion of U.S. jobs requiring on-site work in factories, healthcare, restaurants, and transport
80 percent: Proportion of global jobs requiring on-site work
